## Outcome
Publish an inspectable, normalized `P(opponent_move | position, next-opponent profile)` for each reachable opponent position, using cached raw sources and rating/time-control mixtures. Rating/profile changes should normally be a cheap recomposition, not trigger new Explorer calls or Maia inference.

## Requirements
1. Consume versioned per-position legal move inventories and **independently versioned** Explorer counts and Maia predictions. The algorithm must not equate unavailable/failed/stale with observed zero.
2. Map the profile's opponent-rating distribution and prospective speed mixture to each source's **actual** supported cohorts. Clearly distinguish genuine interpolation/mixture from fabricated fine-grained source evidence. Maia may not condition on speed; record that limitation rather than duplicating predictions as independent measurements.
3. Start with an interpretable Bayesian/pseudocount blend: Explorer likelihood weighted by its effective sample size and a Maia-informed prior, plus a documented fallback when only one source is valid. Compare the existing `blend_probabilities(... prior_games=200)` as a baseline; do not hard-code 200 as proven optimal.
4. Return a full legal-move probability distribution (including uncatalogued replies), source/effective-sample weights, applicability, freshness, algorithm version, and an explicit confidence/quality indicator. If neither source is usable, return an **unknown**/fallback state rather than pretend low-information equal weights are calibrated.
5. Cache/version the derived distribution by underlying source-generation IDs, profile digest/cohort mixture and fusion algorithm version. Reuse shared source caches when the learner rating changes; batch cheaply with bounded reads and no network calls.
6. Retain the last complete coherent publication when refreshed sources are only partially available. Source-specific freshness must be visible; coordinate with existing #8/#4 behaviors without rewriting Opportunities here.

## Acceptance tests
- All legal moves (including uncovered ones) have nonnegative finite probabilities summing to 1 within tolerance where a distribution is published.
- Explorer-only, Maia-only, both, neither, older-complete vs newer-partial, sparse-count, and contradictory-source fixtures have truthful statuses and correct weighting.
- New opponent-profile digest produces a different personalized mixture from the same raw position/source cache, **without** any new external/model request.
- Distinct rating/speed mixtures and unsupported-cohort fallbacks are reproducible; no source loss silently changes an observed zero into unknown or vice versa.
- Worker restart, generation change and partial batch publication do not produce mixed provenance; focused unit plus disposable PostgreSQL tests.

## Non-goals
No UI, no live calls from training, no card selection, no learned opaque ranking model, no full-game tree expansion.

## Starting code
`backend/app/services/introduction_priorities.py::_move_probability`, `repertoire_coverage.blend_probabilities`, and coverage evidence publication. Verify current main.

body:
## Purpose — coordination issue, not a single implementation PR

**Goal:** Optimize the chance that Tempo's user is prepared in their *next actual game*, given their current Lichess rating/time control, the opponent continuations likely at that strength, their current repertoire, and their demonstrated recall. The optimization must adapt automatically as their rating changes. Do **not** substitute a fixed aspirational rating (for example, 1800) for the next-opponent distribution.

**Curriculum direction (2026-10-08 decision):** Card progression should be driven principally by the probability and marginal value of the *next decision*, **not** a fixed move depth or a strict requirement for every parent prefix to reach FSRS `mature`. Keep the learner's decisions in meaningful route sequence (exposure before dependent continuation, or justified gameplay evidence), but treat maturity/weakness as a *soft* readiness input. A high-probability line may advance much deeper than a rare side line. Rare lines deserve some familiarity, not compulsory equal depth. This is intentional **future behavior**: #118 specifies a read-only frontier and #114 performs the eventual guarded switch; current maturity-gated code remains unchanged.

**New global-allocation decision (2026-10-10):** The eventual opening curriculum allocates up to one shared user-configurable number of new cards per day (e.g. 50 across eight repertoires, *not* 10 each). Repertoire weights encode **desired learning priority**, not how frequently the learner expects to select a repertoire in play. Weighted policy-conditioned reach is a useful interpretable baseline; #113 also tests weighted marginal preparedness value. Shared cards consume one introduction slot; #159 defines quota/accounting and review-load backpressure. The new production mode has **no per-repertoire caps/floors**, while the legacy per-repertoire quotas remain intact behind rollback. Only #114 writes production admissions. #157–#160 define bounded independent implementation work.

This roadmap first creates a durable, reusable source-backed move-probability layer; only after shadow evaluation should it change which new opening cards get admitted. Keep individual PRs bounded and independently testable.

### Explicit scope and interpretation

- **Position universe:** distinct *opponent-to-move positions appearing on imported repertoire routes* (canonical board identity; transpositions deduplicated). Evaluate **all legal opponent moves at those positions**, including moves absent from the repertoire. Do *not* recursively expand a full game tree beyond the repertoire.
- **Opponent model:** separate rating/time-control contexts for rapid, blitz, etc. Start from available Lichess rating and empirical recent opponent-rating differences, with auditable cold-start/stale/unknown handling; avoid assuming the next time control is known.
- **Evidence:** Lichess Explorer counts/probabilities for its **actual available rating/speed cohorts** plus rating-conditioned Maia predictions. Cache source data independently, retain source/model provenance, then estimate an explicit probability distribution, with missing-source fallbacks. Verify API/cohort limitations during implementation instead of assuming arbitrary fine-grained Explorer rating filters exist.
- **Reuse:** shared position/cohort/source-version cache independent of repertoire and learner rating; cheap *derived* personalization when rating or target time-control weights change. Never call Explorer/Maia synchronously in the daily-queue or training request.
- **Preparedness:** distinguish (a) repertoire coverage—the probability a supported answer exists at a reached decision—from (b) recall-weighted readiness—the probability the user can produce it. Both should be horizon-specific; expected first unprepared decision/depth is a useful secondary output. Initial recall estimation may be coarse and must be identified as such.
- **Candidate selection and progression:** use expected *marginal* next-game preparation benefit to choose among **sequence-consistent** unintroduced cards. Preserve the logical parent/route order, but **do not make formal parent maturity a prerequisite**; verified previous exposure (or justified gameplay familiarity) defines a minimal ordering guard. Parent recall difficulty affects the benefit estimate rather than imposing a categorical lock. Avoid underfilled new-card quotas when all remaining prefixes are learning; no uniform required move depth across branches. Preserve per-repertoire daily limits **only as a legacy rollback behavior**. The target has one global opening-introduction budget (#159), user-selected learning-priority weights (#157), and a single global ranker (#158), while retaining explicit gameplay promotions, durable admissions, review scheduling and active queue/attempt identity.
- **Robustness:** track source freshness, model/algorithm version, coverage of the requested rating/time control, cache invalidation and provenance. Distinguish unavailable data from a genuine estimated zero. A source failing cannot erase valid newer evidence from the other source.
- **Performance:** bounded background batches, resumable generation or incremental fills, no network/model inference inside PostgreSQL transactions, no unbounded per-review full-repertoire recalculations, no huge task payloads. Enrich every relevant position's legal replies as the durable inventory progresses, but fill only requested/neighboring rating and speed cohorts on demand; do not eagerly compute the Cartesian product of all cohorts.

## Current implementation baseline

Verified from `main` at `2dd998b8df9e099c1fa39eec70c522b4db84863e` (2026-10-08); verify again before each PR:

- `backend/app/services/opening_graph.py` and `postgres_opening_graph.py` already create canonical prefix/descendant cards with dependency unlocks. **As of the audited code, ordinary descendant unlocking is gated on `parent.state='mature'`**, which can starve introductions with short prefixes; relaxing this is an explicit, separate policy change, not part of source-cache work.
- `backend/app/services/introduction_priorities.py` currently calculates `0.7 * completion_mass + 0.3 * frontier_reach` with optional gameplay-miss bonus. `repertoire_coverage.blend_probabilities` already provides a basic Explorer/Maia blend.
- `backend/app/main.py::_plan_prioritized_opening_admissions` selects eligible cards; `_plan_daily_queue_order` then **separately shuffles** the daily presentation order. `backend/app/services/postgres_queue_refresh.py` implements the bounded PostgreSQL phases.
- A fresh PostgreSQL PGN import (`pgn_import_commands.py`) schedules graph/integrity/queue work without requiring an initial published priority generation; absent score data can leave tie-breaking to card length/hash. This is an explicit integration gap, not evidence that the existing scoring function is never used.
- Priority publication/replay infrastructure already exists in `postgres_priority.py`; reuse it rather than create a second independent prioritization service.

## Related existing work — coordinate, do not duplicate

- #4: evidence-backed repertoire opportunities (including missing common opponent replies); probability layer should feed its existing input contract where appropriate.
- #3 and #6: Lichess Explorer authentication/session reliability; source acquisition should degrade gracefully while these remain open.
- #8: newer partial/source-specific coverage evidence issue (historically closed, but verify source freshness behavior instead of assuming the bug is resolved).
- #30: prepared/atomic priority generations already implemented; build on that mechanism.
- #40 and #41: input-version refresh coalescing and targeted fan-out; avoid conflicting schedulers.
- #76: adaptive prefix graph and history-preserving transitions; rank existing card identities without imposing new segmentation logic.

## Delivery tracks

These linked issues form a dependency-aware milestone checklist. **#107, #108, and independent learning-weight contract #157 can proceed without waiting on the downstream ranking chain**; other work should wait only on its named contract dependencies. Each child is small enough for an independent review and owns focused acceptance tests.

### Phase A — independent foundations (parallel now)
- [ ] #107 — Next-opponent rating/time-control profile and versioned snapshots (independent)
- [ ] #108 — Canonical opponent-position inventory and every legal reply (independent)
- [ ] #157 — Explicit repertoire learning-priority settings/contract (independent; not inferred play frequency)

### Phase B — durable source caches (parallel after #108)
- [ ] #109 — Explorer count/frequency cache by actual rating and speed cohorts; coordinate #3/#6
- [ ] #110 — Rating-conditioned Maia distribution cache with verified model/runtime semantics

### Phase C — predictive core
- [ ] #111 — Blend source distributions with source-aware fallbacks/calibration (after #107, #109, #110)
- [ ] #112 — Calculate probability-weighted structural coverage, recall-weighted readiness and marginal benefit (after #108, #111)
- [ ] #118 — Model sequence-aware, probability-driven descendant frontiers **without a hard parent-maturity gate**, shadow-only (after #112; before #113)
- [ ] #158 — Build one read-only weighted global ranker for eligible opening cards (after #156/#157/#112/#118)

### Phase D — evaluate, explain, integrate
- [ ] #113 — Shadow-rank the legacy, new conditional, and **global weighted** progression/selection policies against held-out games, with *no admission changes* (after #112/#118/#158)
- [ ] #115 — Minimal user-facing explanations, source coverage and freshness diagnostics (after #111/#112; parallel with #113)
- [ ] #159 — Establish one global daily opening-introduction budget and workload/accounting contract (parallel to #113; cutover owned by #114)
- [ ] #114 — Reversible global opening-card admission **and relaxed descendant progression** cutover with bounded first-import fallback (after successful #113 and #158/#159; coordinate #40/#41)
- [ ] #160 — User-facing learning-weight/global-budget settings and global ranking preview (after #157/#158/#159; coordinate #115)

### Dependency sketch

```text
#107 (opponent profile) ────────────────────────────┐
                                                    v
#108 (position inventory) ─┬─> #109 (Explorer) ─> #111 (fusion)
                            └─> #110 (Maia) ────────┘
             #108 + #111 ────────────> #112 (readiness)
                                          |
                                          v
                                  #118 (relaxed frontier)
                                          |
                                          v
                                  #113 (shadow comparison)
                                   [quality gate]
                                          |
                                          v
                                  #114 (policy switch)

#111 + #112 ───────────────────> #115 (explanations, parallel)
```

**Review/merge cadence:** A/B can be built in parallel after the inventory contract is stable; C/D use feature flags and immutable published snapshots. #114 is the only issue allowed to change normal new-card selection. Existing issues #4, #3/#6, #8, #40/#41 and #76 are adjacent dependencies/constraints, **not** newly duplicated deliverables.

**Release gates:**
1. Source data and personalization are durable, versioned, queryable, and correct with cold-start, missing source, transposition and uncovered-move fixtures.
2. A shadow scorer runs without affecting existing admissions. Held-out next-game move likelihood/calibration and ranking are compared against the current heuristic and simple count-only baselines; choose thresholds based on measured baselines, not invented improvement percentages.
3. Only then enable the **joint ranking + relaxed progression** policy behind a reversible feature flag, with bounded waiting/fallback for a just-imported repertoire, reproducible explanations, no active-queue reorder, and explicit no-starvation tests for very short prefixes. Maturity cannot remain a hard gate under the new policy.
4. Verify full disposable-PostgreSQL lifecycle, interruptions, current-deployment upgrade, source failure, and latency/no-regression tests.

## Non-goals for the initial release

- Learning a personalized chess move generator from scratch or requiring GPU inference.
- Changing FSRS state from a probabilistic guess, inventing reviews, or treating game deviations as controlled retrieval failures.
- Automatic changes to prefix sizes or wholesale replacement of the existing opportunities/discoveries engine.
- A complex learned learning-cost optimizer before actual learning effort is measurable.
- Claiming a particular move probability is precise when source cohorts are coarse or unsupported.

**Final product north star:** “Given whom I am likely to play next, how likely am I to know what to play through move N, and which available card improves that the most?”

## Repertoire-choice conditioning (2026-10-10 clarification)

**Mandatory semantic contract:** Path reach and marginal new-card value within a selected repertoire are **conditional on the learner choosing that repertoire's defining route**, not on the unconditional frequency of that route across all the learner's imported repertoires. Example: an Italian repertoire beginning `1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4` and a Ruy Lopez repertoire beginning `1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5` may coexist. Italian internal priorities use `P(reach decision | learner chooses Italian at the defining choice, opponent profile)`; Ruy Lopez internal priorities analogously condition on choosing Bb5. Do not infer the learner's choice probability from the presence or number of imported PGNs, duplicate routes, or source-game frequencies.

The opponent's move probabilities remain position/cohort-specific, shared across repertoires, and normalized over **all legal opponent replies**. The conditioning is applied when propagating route reach mass through the learner's *chosen* responses. A repertoire selection is an explicit route policy/context, not a new probability model or a request to renormalize opponent moves over authored lines. When an opening has an opponent deviation **before** the defining learner move, retain its probability as uncovered/early-exit mass under an explicitly stated starting-event convention; do not pretend every game reaches the choice. For **unconditional next-game probability** comparisons across repertoires, require genuine repertoire-choice frequencies or show separate conditional scores; never pretend the study weights are measured choice frequencies. For **global study allocation**, use explicit learner-selected priority weights (#157) to combine policy-conditioned candidate benefits into an explicitly labeled *study score* (#158).

Implement/verify primarily in #112 (reachability and marginal value), #113 (shadow ordering), #118 (frontier), and #115 (explanations).

Connect the branch comparison preview to the durable shorter-prefix application workflow with truthful confirmation, pending/recovery states, and post-publication verification.

## Requirements

- **Selection:** explicit source routes / line IDs tied to a current authoritative snapshot.

Tempo's CLI creates revision-specific local application image tags and per-operation release snapshots, but has no retirement step. Repeated successful updates or failed image preparation can accumulate Docker Desktop storage and state directories indefinitely.

Related implementation: [PR #73](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/73). This is a separate operational follow-up and does not block that PR's credential-validation fix. No historical images or releases were deleted while investigating it.

Current structure in `scripts/tempo-runtime.mjs::ensureImages()`:

- Built application tags use `${target.project}-${service}:tempo-${revision}` with `org.opencontainers.image.revision` labels.
- Release directories use `<target state>/releases/<revision>-<operation-id>/`, containing copied Compose definitions, build-label overlays, and immutable `images.json` overlays.
- `deployment.json` records the current verified revision, immutable image IDs, `composeFiles`, `imageOverride`, configuration fingerprint, CI evidence, and backup reference. Compatible starts and verified fallback depend on these artifacts.
- `operation.json` identifies the current attempt, revision, phase/failed phase, and backup/history references. An unresolved `migration-guard.json` retains origin/last-attempted revisions, attempt ID, original H0, and verified backup. Retention must not remove artifacts needed to understand or continue those obligations.

Implement bounded, ownership-aware retirement without changing database recovery behavior:

1. After a successful deployment, identify unreferenced historical CLI release directories and owned revision tags, then retire only artifacts proven unnecessary for the current deployment, running/stopped containers, permitted fallback, or unresolved operations/migrations.
2. After failed image preparation, retire owned unused partial-candidate tags and release snapshots when their references and recovery/diagnostic requirements have been checked. Keep the last verified deployment usable and preserve unresolved operation/guard evidence.
3. Verify exact target/daemon/project/checkout/revision ownership and references immediately before deletion. Preserve uncertain ownership or references and provide useful diagnostics. Do not infer ownership from age or tag spelling alone.
4. Never globally prune Docker or force-remove shared image IDs. Retain shared/base images and build caches, artifacts used by other tasks/targets, live study resources, backups, and authoritative data volumes. If an owned tag refers to a shared image ID, do not remove another owner's references.
5. Add named regular regressions for current-receipt preservation, unresolved guard/operation preservation, active container/shared-image references, successful-update cleanup, failed-preparation cleanup, and safe idempotent interruption/retry. Cover actual Docker ownership/reference behavior where mocked checks cannot prove it, and register coverage in `tests/REGRESSIONS.md`.

Acceptance: repeated successful and failed candidates no longer accumulate unreferenced owned artifacts without bound; the recorded deployment still starts through immutable fallback; unresolved migration recovery/evidence remains intact; cleanup can be rerun safely; no global pruning or unrelated resource deletion occurs. Choose a minimal retention policy based on these concrete reference requirements, and document diagnostics and retained-artifact reasons.
title: Retire unreferenced Tempo deployment images and release directories safely

1. Separate disposable wake-up notifications from durable work. Parent #29. **Prerequisites: #30 and #39** (and transitively #38). Build on their prepared-generation and nonblocking dispatch/admission seams.

## Proposed contract to implement

Use a narrow refresh-intent model with concepts such as requested input version, prepared/running version, published version, first dirty time, last dirty time, next eligible time, and invalidation reason. Exact schema is flexible; reuse existing tables/checkpoints.

- Same semantic input/version requested again: no-op, not a new generation.
- New relevant input while queued: advance the requested watermark and coalesce the pending calculation.
- New input while running: retain useful work where safe and record at most one required successor targeting the newest known watermark. Do not silently erase a lease or cursor on each request.
- Structural invalidation, deleted data, incompatible scoring/policy changes, or revoked training eligibility: immediately prevent invalid/stale authoritative use. These are not merely advisory ranking refreshes.
- A trailing quiet period must have a maximum scheduling delay anchored to the first unserved dirty event. Proposed initial experiment: 15–30 seconds quiet, 1–2 minutes maximum delay. Make defaults explicit and tested; these are recommendations, not existing guarantees.
- The maximum is an eligibility/scheduling bound, not an unconditional completion promise under worker failure or unlimited load. Expose requested/published versions and stale/pending state honestly.
- Time-dependent scoring must use a stable as-of boundary/version and a deliberate refresh cadence; do not compare a continuously drifting wall-clock output hash as input identity.

## Correctness requirements

1. Record dirty intent in the same transaction as the relevant data publication, or an equally reliable existing transactional mechanism. A dropped process-local timer cannot lose refresh work.
2. Prevent the publish-vs-new-input race from erasing a newer request; compare-and-set/fence version transitions and publication pointers.
3. Define where last-complete advisory results may remain readable while refreshing and where integrity/eligibility requires invalidation. Preserve dismissal semantics (#7), source-specific freshness/provenance (#8), and gameplay-vs-FSRS separation (#4).
4. User reviews/grades, teaching events, edits/import persistence, accepted admissions, raw game ingestion, engine reports/releases, and receipt recovery remain prompt and durable. Do not route them through this quiet window.
5. Unknown/unclassified task kinds keep existing semantics. Keep a small explicit policy table/allowlist rather than inferring importance from task names.
6. Avoid unbounded generation rows, event growth, delayed broker messages, or per-event full signature scans. Reuse the retention and recovery lifecycle.

- [ ] A burst of duplicate same-version requests produces one calculation/publication and no progress resets.
- [ ] A burst of increasing versions coalesces; an event during execution yields at most one successor representing the latest watermark.
- [ ] Continuous arrivals cannot keep pushing the first dirty eligibility beyond the configured maximum; frozen-clock tests verify exact behavior.
- [ ] Crash/restart preserves dirty intent and eligibility; a lost wake-up is recovered.
- [ ] Publication concurrent with a new request cannot clear that request or publish mixed input versions.
- [ ] Structural invalidation/deletion blocks invalid content immediately; explicit user commands are not delayed.
- [ ] Dismissal, partial source freshness, scoring parity, and authoritative training eligibility remain correct.
- [ ] Compare generations started/restarted/discarded, useful publications, and observed freshness under synthetic bursts using #37 metrics.

## Outcome / PR boundary

A task denied background admission must yield its worker slot instead of waiting indefinitely for foreground activity to end. Preserve foreground responsiveness and reliable control callbacks. Parent #29. **Implement after #38** to build on execution-time claiming rather than creating a second dispatch lifecycle. #37 provides useful wait/progress diagnostics.

This PR changes admission/deferral behavior only. It does not change analysis formulas, global task concurrency, database timeout defaults, or engine scheduling policy.

## Source mechanism

Audit revision `9dec8735fcc377e70ae3e2633870a81dfd3ebff2`; verify current main:

- [redis_admission_gate.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/9dec8735fcc377e70ae3e2633870a81dfd3ebff2/backend/app/services/redis_admission_gate.py): `background_lease` loops with 10 ms sleeps until foreground leases disappear.
- [activity_gate.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/9dec8735fcc377e70ae3e2633870a81dfd3ebff2/backend/app/services/activity_gate.py): background database sections wait for foreground; browser activity defaults to a 3-second window.
- `app/views/home_view.tsx` sends throttled activity on pointerdown/keydown; `docker-compose.yml` configures one background worker process.
- Inspect `database_executor.py`, PostgreSQL connection wrappers, `tasks.py`, durable-task deferral, command-gateway operation retries, and background HTTP callback classification.

Frequent user activity can keep a worker waiting rather than computing. Other background messages then wait behind it. Low CPU plus a queue can therefore be starvation, not necessarily inadequate capacity.

## Required design

1. Introduce a small nonblocking/bounded admission result at the existing seam. Distinguish deferred-for-foreground from execution failure and from database contention; no indefinite busy wait or thread sleeping inside an occupied Celery task.
2. Check admission before heavy work. If denied, retain durable intent, record an eligible retry time with bounded jitter/backoff, and return. Repeated denials must coalesce, not create unlimited Celery countdown/wake messages or exhaust error retries.
3. Define the narrow bookkeeping path needed to persist a deferral/receipt without itself recursively waiting for the admission it is recording. Keep those writes short and fenced; do not make all background SQL effectively foreground.
4. Classify essential control work separately from discretionary analysis: already-accepted command receipts, engine report/release callbacks, durable recovery, and operations needed to finish a user command must not deadlock behind a browser heartbeat. Keep actual request/transaction contention protection and correct work-class accounting.
5. Preserve rollback/no-partial-commit behavior if foreground arrives between bounded stages. Never redo expensive preparation on each harmless admission denial when a safe checkpoint already exists.
6. Specify a conservative fairness policy for eligible discretionary work: aging and a bounded progress budget when capacity exists, while preserving strict foreground latency budgets. Browser activity is a scheduling hint, not permission to hide a dependent operation indefinitely. Do not promise progress under physically unlimited foreground load.
7. Handle expired/crashed foreground leases and Redis outages explicitly. Retain safe failure behavior, clear diagnostics, and eventual recovery; never silently allow unsafe writes because the gate is unavailable.

## Regression acceptance

- [ ] Sustained activity returns a denied task promptly without holding a worker slot; a following eligible control task can execute.
- [ ] A foreground request waiting on a background publication/receipt cannot create a dependency deadlock with the gate.
- [ ] Many denials create bounded durable state/messages and do not consume terminal failure retry counts or reset useful work.
- [ ] After activity ceases, eligible work resumes and the oldest pending age decreases; stale browser/foreground leases recover after crashes.
- [ ] Under a controlled mixed workload, foreground latency remains within existing budgets and eligible background work makes measurable progress.
- [ ] Task/command generation fencing, transaction rollback, idempotent receipts, pause controls, and restart replay remain correct.
- [ ] Redis failure and admission/foreground races have explicit tested behavior; no recursive bookkeeping deadlock.
- [ ] Count wait occupancy, deferrals, messages, useful completions, and foreground latency before/after using #37 or equivalent focused measurements.

## Agent execution

Read `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`; isolated branch/checkout based on merged #38. Add named regular-suite regressions and update `tests/REGRESSIONS.md`. Use focused Python/task tests and disposable PostgreSQL/Redis/Celery concurrency checks, then required final `make full` with documented permissions. Do not mutate or reset live queues. Report work-class policy, denial persistence, fairness bounds, retry semantics, race coverage, measured tradeoffs, and blocked validation. Any larger scheduling redesign needs a separate issue.

Current [backend/app/services/threat_training.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/5dd0815b4bac42dea3077959fd92f1db33f4cf04/backend/app/services/threat_training.py) and persistence regressions include bounded/restartable validation, approval/attempt idempotency and capped automatic admission ranked by recurring position. That is not proof of the requested distinct-game motif/subtype aggregation and one explicit recurring-pattern pack with user approval. Next action: reconcile the auto-admission/recognition behavior with this issue and #13, and provide the specified three-game end-to-end recommendation regression before closure. Keep open.

<!-- /issue-pr-review-20261002 -->

## Objective

Connect the defensive-threat pipeline end to end and surface repeated real-game weaknesses as personalized training priorities.

This is the final integration issue for the first knight-fork prototype.

## Pipeline

The complete flow should be:

```text
imported game
→ existing game analysis
→ defensive threat seed
→ actual learner anchors
→ background validation
→ durable candidate
→ recurrence aggregation
→ user approval / training
→ controlled study result
```

No stage should fabricate evidence for a later stage.

## Service boundary

Add an orchestration service with operations conceptually like:

```python
class ThreatTrainingService:
    def detect_game(self, game_id: str) -> tuple[str, ...]: ...
    def validate_anchor(self, candidate_id: str) -> ValidationResult: ...
    def approve_exercise(self, candidate_id: str) -> str: ...
    def submit_attempt(
        self,
        exercise_id: str,
        exercise_revision: str,
        attempt_id: str,
        move_uci: str,
    ) -> MoveGrade: ...
```

The exact class/function organization may differ, but orchestration must remain separate from pure chess detection/validation functions.

## Background-work requirements

Follow Tempo's existing foreground-first rules:

- bounded DB reads/writes;
- no long engine work inside SQLite transactions;
- reuse compatible analysis before requesting more;
- enqueue missing engine analysis;
- yield to interactive engine/training work;
- version-check before publication;
- resumable/idempotent durable tasks.

Extend the existing engine broker/request path to support the analysis options needed by validation, including restricted root moves where required.

Do not create a second unmanaged Stockfish worker.

## Recurring-pattern aggregation

Aggregate validated incidents by motif/subtype over an explicit recent window.

For v1, a simple deterministic threshold is sufficient, for example:

```text
distinct supporting games with validated knight-fork defensive failure >= 3
→ surface recurring-pattern recommendation
```

Important:

- count distinct incidents/supporting games;
- multiple precursor anchors from one game/fork count once;
- do not infer a prevention/failure rate from a dataset containing only failures;
- retain rapid/blitz metadata so future reporting can compare them.

Suggested summary fields:

```text
motif
subtype
incident_count
supporting_game_ids
recent_incident_count
average_consequence_cp
latest_occurrence
approved_exercise_count
```

## User-facing recommendation

Surface a compact recommendation such as:

> Recurring defensive pattern: incoming knight fork
>
> Seen in 4 recent games. Drill 3 positions from your games.

Do not automatically flood the daily queue with every generated anchor.

Prefer one explicit recommendation / pack-style entry from which the user can approve or begin drills.

## Observability

Background activity should make it possible to distinguish:

- detecting;
- waiting for engine analysis;
- validating;
- ready;
- failed/inconclusive.

Do not expose raw engine internals or produce noisy per-position UI.

## Regression coverage

Add an end-to-end fixture covering:

1. imported game contains/permits checking knight fork;
2. one or more real learner anchors are generated;
3. missing engine work is queued;
4. foreground engine request can preempt background work;
5. validation resumes idempotently;
6. candidate is published once;
7. repeated failures across 3 distinct games produce one recurring-pattern recommendation;
8. multiple anchors from one incident do not inflate recurrence;
9. approval creates/reuses training object once;
10. completed attempt flows through normal scheduling exactly once.

Also test restart/replay behavior for durable tasks and stale analysis versions.

## Out of scope

Do not expand this first integration into:

- general strategic-plan understanding;
- LLM-based motif classification;
- learned/ML recommendation ranking;
- every tactical motif;
- automatic causal claims about training effectiveness;
- generalized event sourcing.

The next motif should reuse this architecture only after the knight-fork path works end to end.

## Definition of done

Tempo automatically turns repeated, engine-supported defensive knight-fork failures from real games into an auditable personalized training recommendation and can deliver/grade those exercises without interfering with foreground play or conflating gameplay evidence with FSRS memory evidence.
title: Add durable background orchestration and recurring-pattern promotion for defensive threat training

[PR #16](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/16), [PR #24](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/24) and [PR #27](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/27) are PostgreSQL/receipt/recovery follow-ups.

[backend/tests/test_defensive_threat_grading.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/5dd0815b4bac42dea3077959fd92f1db33f4cf04/backend/tests/test_defensive_threat_grading.py) and [backend/tests/test_defensive_threat_persistence.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/5dd0815b4bac42dea3077959fd92f1db33f4cf04/backend/tests/test_defensive_threat_persistence.py) cover sound alternatives, unlisted-root analysis, motif attribution, ambiguous/illegal outcomes, exactly-once scheduling and stale revisions. However the persistence test expects “What danger should your next move account for?”, while this issue specifies “Choose your move.” and excludes the later two-step recognition mode. The current recognition workflow must be reconciled with the issue before declaring full completion; passing grading tests alone do not settle that product decision.

Reviewed against main `5dd0815b4bac42dea3077959fd92f1db33f4cf04`, all pre-existing open PRs, and merged PRs from September 18–October 2. Issue state is unchanged by this audit.

<!-- /issue-pr-review-20261002 -->

## Objective

Turn an engine-supported defensive-threat candidate into an actual training exercise and grade the learner's move without requiring one memorized engine move.

This issue is the first user-facing training vertical slice.

## Exercise UX

Initial exercise prompt should be deliberately minimal:

> Choose your move.

Do not reveal `incoming knight fork` before the answer. The purpose is to train threat recognition, not motif recall after being told the motif.

After grading, feedback may explain:

- the relevant knight route;
- fork destination;
- attacked king/major piece;
- why the historical/attempted move failed;
- one or more sound defensive ideas.

A later two-step "identify the threat, then move" mode is out of scope for v1.

## Proposed objects

Add concepts equivalent to:

- `DefenseExercise`
- `MoveGrade`

`DefenseExercise` should pin:

- candidate/finding ID;
- exercise revision;
- anchor position context;
- policy snapshot;
- best known score;
- evaluated root moves;
- refutation line.

## Grading contract

Implement conceptually:

```python
def grade_defense_move(
    exercise: DefenseExercise,
    move_uci: str,
    *,
    additional_analysis: AnalysisReport | None = None,
) -> MoveGrade:
    ...
```

Required outcomes:

- `correct`
- `incorrect`
- `needs_analysis`
- `ambiguous`
- `illegal`

## Critical rule: MultiPV is not the answer key

A legal submitted move absent from the saved MultiPV must not automatically be marked wrong.

Instead:

1. if already evaluated with compatible analysis, compare its learner-oriented score with best;
2. if legal but not sufficiently evaluated, return `needs_analysis` and request a root-move-constrained analysis;
3. only issue a definitive incorrect grade after sufficient evidence.

Suggested initial finite-score policy:

- <= 30cp from best → correct;
- >= 100cp worse → incorrect;
- between thresholds → ambiguous / require stronger confirmation.

These are tunable policy defaults, not chess truths.

## Motif attribution

Store separately:

- whether the move is good/bad;
- whether it specifically allows the target knight-fork motif.

A submitted move may be bad for another reason. Do not tell the learner they missed a knight fork unless the validating refutation actually demonstrates that motif.

Likewise, a sound move may leave the geometric fork available but have adequate compensation or a stronger tactical answer.

## Scheduling boundary

Only a definitive controlled study grade may update the card's normal review/FSRS path.

Do not create an FSRS failure for:

- illegal UI input;
- `needs_analysis`;
- `ambiguous`;
- engine timeout/failure;
- stale exercise revision.

Use an `attempt_id` for idempotency. A retry after network failure must not schedule twice.

## Card integration

Approved candidates should create or reuse a training card representing a defensive-move rubric.

Do not force this into one exact `moves_json` continuation if that would imply only one legal answer is correct.

Keep the source finding/candidate association so feedback remains auditable.

## Regression coverage

At minimum:

1. Engine best move → correct.
2. Different sound move within tolerance → correct.
3. Legal unanalysed move → needs analysis, not wrong.
4. Clearly losing move with verified target fork → incorrect with fork feedback.
5. Bad move for unrelated reason → incorrect but no false knight-fork explanation.
6. Illegal move → no FSRS update.
7. Engine timeout on submitted move → no FSRS update.
8. Ambiguous threshold case → no punitive scheduling.
9. Duplicate attempt submission → one scheduling update.
10. Stale exercise revision → reject/reload rather than grade against old rubric.

Update `tests/REGRESSIONS.md`.

## Definition of done

A user can train one defensive knight-fork precursor position, play any reasonable legal defense, receive an engine-backed grade, and only definitive study outcomes affect scheduling.
title: Create defensive-move exercises with engine-backed alternative-move grading

## Summary

Follow-up to #3.

Tempo now authenticates Explorer requests, but the backend coverage path keeps the registered Lichess token only in process memory. The browser separately remembers that it already registered the current token. This can leave background repertoire coverage idle after a backend restart.

## Failure sequence

Browser has valid Lichess session token → browser registers token with backend → backend stores token only in process memory → backend restarts and loses it → browser remains open and token value is unchanged → browser does not re-register → backend refuses Explorer coverage work because no token is registered.

## Relevant code

- `app/hooks/use-repertoire-coverage.ts`
- `backend/app/services/repertoire_coverage.py`
- Explorer-session endpoint in `backend/app/main.py`

## Desired behavior

A backend restart or loss of backend session registration should recover without requiring a page reload, a new OAuth flow, or a changed browser token.

Keep the distinction between:

1. backend registration missing — the existing browser credential may be re-registered;
2. credential rejected by Lichess (401/403) — do not blindly retry the same bad token; require reconnection as appropriate.

Do not persist the raw OAuth token to durable application storage merely to solve this unless there is a compelling reason.

## Suggested direction

Use the smallest explicit contract that lets the frontend determine whether the backend currently has Explorer authentication registered. A status endpoint, registration generation/session identifier, or safe idempotent re-registration strategy would all be reasonable.

## Regression coverage

Add a named regression covering: browser holds a valid token; backend registration is established; backend in-memory token is reset/restarted; browser token remains unchanged; frontend re-registers it; background coverage becomes claimable again.

Also verify 401/403 still requires reconnect behavior, repeated registration is idempotent, and token values never appear in logs, diagnostics, URLs, cache keys, or persisted coverage state. Update `tests/REGRESSIONS.md`.

## Definition of done

Restarting the backend while Tempo remains open does not strand repertoire coverage in an unauthenticated idle state.

The named `test_issue4_*` regressions in [backend/tests/test_repertoire_opportunities.py](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/blob/5dd0815b4bac42dea3077959fd92f1db33f4cf04/backend/tests/test_repertoire_opportunities.py) cover strong-route promotion, weak evidence, transpositions, personal replies, post-gap findings and foreground/replay behavior; the regular registry also names the UI proof. <!-- /issue-pr-review-20261002 -->

## Objective

Build a durable **Repertoire Opportunities** layer that turns Tempo's existing evidence into concrete, auditable recommendations about what opening knowledge should be trained or added next.

This should synthesize infrastructure Tempo already has:

- canonical opening graph and decision identity;
- opening-card dependency/progression;
- real-game `repertoire_decision_events`;
- game repertoire matching and findings;
- introduction priorities;
- repertoire coverage;
- personal game-position occurrences;
- Maia probabilities;
- Lichess Opening Explorer probabilities;
- Stockfish/game-analysis evidence;
- background/durable work infrastructure.

The product question is:

> Given the repertoire I intend to play, what opponents at my level actually play, what I already demonstrate successfully in real games, and where I fail, what specific repertoire/training intervention has the highest practical value?

Do not build a learned recommendation model yet. Start with explicit, inspectable evidence and deterministic rules.

---

# Core design principle: dependencies are defaults, not absolute barriers

The canonical graph currently encodes progressive learning dependencies:

```text
prefix
  ↓
decision 7
  ↓
decision 8
  ↓
decision 9
```

That remains the correct **default curriculum**.

However, real gameplay can provide evidence that the learner already possesses prerequisite knowledge even when those prerequisites have not formally matured through Tempo.

Example:

```text
Decisions 1–6:
  encountered 14 times
  correct 13/14

Decision 7:
  encountered 9 times
  correct 2/9
```

If decision 7 already exists in the repertoire but is locked behind decisions 1–6, forcing the learner to formally complete 1–6 before addressing decision 7 wastes strong real-world evidence.

Tempo should therefore support:

```text
parent maturity
    → normal unlock

OR

strong gameplay reach + weakness evidence
    → evidence-backed early promotion
```

Crucially:

**Early promotion does not mean prerequisite mastery.**

Do not manufacture FSRS reviews or mark prerequisite cards mature merely because gameplay suggests familiarity.

Keep separate:

1. controlled study/memory state;
2. observed gameplay competence;
3. curriculum admission/unlock state.

This follows the same epistemic separation being established for the real-game feedback loop.

---

# Initial opportunity types

Implement the opportunity model around exactly three initial types.

## 1. Weak known decision

The repertoire already contains the correct decision/card.

Evidence pattern:

```text
canonical decision exists
+ card is locked/unintroduced or otherwise low priority
+ position is repeatedly reached in real games
+ earlier route decisions are usually successful
+ this decision is repeatedly missed
```

Action:

> Promote the existing canonical card for training, potentially bypassing its normal parent-maturity gate.

Example explanation:

> Promoted because you reached this decision 11 times recently and missed it 7 times.

Do not create a duplicate card.

Do not mark its parents mature.

Do not mutate FSRS state until controlled study actually occurs.

---

## 2. Missing common opponent response

At a canonical opponent node, a practically important move is not represented in the repertoire.

Evidence can come from:

- Maia probability for the user's approximate cohort;
- Lichess Explorer probability for an appropriate rating/speed cohort;
- the user's own games;
- reach probability for the position.

Example:

```text
Position P

Opponent responses:

...Nf6   42%   covered
...e6    27%   covered
...c5    11%   NOT covered
...Bf5    7%   NOT covered
...Nh5    4%   NOT covered
```

Tempo should surface practically important uncovered responses.

This is particularly important because high-level authored repertoires may omit moves that titled players consider inaccurate but which are common at lower ratings.

A move being objectively inferior is **not** a reason to ignore it if the user encounters it frequently.

Action:

> Propose a repertoire branch for investigation/addition.

Do not silently mutate the repertoire in the first version.

---

## 3. Post-gap weakness

An opponent plays an uncovered/unprincipled response, and the learner subsequently struggles.

Pattern:

```text
opponent plays uncovered move
        ↓
player continues without prepared coverage
        ↓
within next few player decisions
        ↓
large/repeated mistake
```

Tempo already has the beginning of this in `game_findings.py`: after a repertoire gap it examines subsequent player decisions, detects sufficiently large engine mistakes, creates a `repertoire gap` finding, and can link an unseen existing card.

Reuse and generalize this rather than creating a competing subsystem.

Action:

> Surface an opportunity to investigate/add a response, with the game and engine evidence attached.

---

# Make gameplay reach a first-class signal

For each canonical learner decision, derive useful gameplay evidence such as:

- encounter count;
- success count;
- miss count;
- success rate;
- recent encounter count;
- last encountered;
- successful route/prerequisite traversal count;
- number of times the learner successfully reached this decision.

This should be derived from durable historical facts such as `repertoire_decision_events`, not by mutating FSRS state.

The system should distinguish:

| Evidence | Interpretation | Default action |
|---|---|---|
| Rarely/never reached | Low evidence | normal graph progression |
| Frequently reached and usually correct | likely implicit competence | lower urgency / useful prerequisite evidence |
| Frequently reached and frequently wrong | high-value weakness | promote target |

Avoid treating tiny samples as strong evidence.

Use explicit minimum-count thresholds initially rather than statistical sophistication.

---

# Evidence-backed descendant promotion

Implement a narrow exception to graph admission.

A locked/unintroduced descendant may become trainable early when gameplay evidence demonstrates both:

1. **reach competence**: the learner repeatedly navigates the prerequisite route successfully;
2. **target weakness**: the target decision itself is repeatedly missed.

This should affect admission/priority, not memory state.

Conceptually:

```text
normal:
parent mature → child eligible

exception:
parent not formally mature
+ repeated successful real-game traversal
+ repeated target misses
→ child eligible via gameplay evidence
```

Persist/derive the reason so the UI can explain the exception.

Example:

> Priority introduction · reached 9 times in games, missed 6 times.

Do not allow one anomalous game to bypass the curriculum.

Choose conservative initial thresholds and make them constants/settings that can be tuned later.

---

# Integration checkpoints

Early isolated promotion creates one legitimate risk: the learner may know a decision in isolation without being able to reconstruct the full route deliberately.

Preserve the canonical graph's integration role.

If a descendant is introduced early through gameplay evidence:

- do not alter its ancestry;
- do not mark ancestors mature;
- retain normal graph progression;
- allow later cumulative/integration review to verify the route.

Do not overbuild a new checkpoint system if the existing cumulative-prefix/hybrid graph already provides an appropriate integration mechanism.

Document how the promoted decision eventually rejoins normal progression.

---

# Coverage scouting

Extend the existing coverage concepts from:

> How complete is this repertoire?

toward:

> Which uncovered opponent moves matter enough to investigate?

For each relevant opponent node, retain/derive:

- probability of reaching the position;
- opponent-move probability;
- whether the move is covered;
- Maia probability;
- Explorer probability;
- personal occurrence count/frequency;
- sample/provenance status;
- cohort information;
- stale/pending/failed evidence status.

Do not report false precision when Maia/Explorer data are unavailable or stale.

The system should rank missing coverage based on **practical relevance**, not Masters frequency alone.

---

# Lower-level/common mistake coverage

This is a first-class use case.

Strong authored repertoires often omit opponent moves because they are objectively inaccurate or considered easy to punish.

For the target user population, those moves may nevertheless be common and nontrivial to exploit correctly.

Tempo should be capable of identifying cases such as:

```text
Masters:        0.3%
Lichess cohort: 7%
Maia cohort:    9%
Personal games: 5 / 42
Repertoire:     uncovered
```

That is a potentially valuable repertoire opportunity despite near-zero Masters frequency.

The system should not equate:

```text
objectively bad opponent move
=
irrelevant move
```

Frequency and practical consequence matter.

---

# Roles of the evidence sources

Keep the evidence semantics explicit.

### Personal games

Answer:

> What am I actually encountering and where am I actually failing?

As personal sample size grows, this should become especially valuable.

### Lichess Explorer

Answer:

> What do players in a relevant rating/speed population actually play?

Use the repaired authenticated Explorer integration from the relevant Explorer issue.

### Maia

Answer:

> What moves are plausible for human players around the relevant skill level?

Particularly useful for estimating opponent behavior where Explorer samples are weak or for smoothing.

### Masters Explorer

Useful context for strong-player/theoretical play, but should **not** dominate practical lower-rating coverage decisions.

### Stockfish

Answer:

> How should this move/position be handled, and how consequential was the learner's response?

Do not use Stockfish to enumerate every legal inferior opponent move. Practical-frequency evidence should gate expensive analysis.

---

# Avoid combinatorial repertoire expansion

Do not crawl every legal opponent move and create branches.

A missing opponent move should only become a candidate when practical evidence clears a gate, e.g. one or more of:

- cohort probability >= threshold;
- personal encounter count >= threshold;
- personal frequency >= threshold;
- repeated post-gap mistakes;
- sufficient cumulative uncovered probability mass.

The exact initial thresholds should be simple, conservative, and inspectable.

Analysis should follow practical relevance, not precede it.

---

# Initial scoring

Do not use ML.

Use deterministic, interpretable scoring/ranking.

For a known decision, something conceptually like:

```text
promotion_score
  = reach_evidence
  × weakness
  × recency
```

where weakness is related to observed miss rate.

For a missing branch:

```text
gap_score
  = P(reach position)
  × P(opponent move | position)
  × personal relevance
  × consequence
```

For the first implementation, `consequence` may be 1 unless post-gap game/engine evidence exists.

The exact formula can differ if existing introduction-priority machinery provides a cleaner integration.

More important than the formula: store enough component evidence that a recommendation can say **why** it ranked highly.

Do not expose only an opaque score.

---

# Durable Repertoire Opportunity model

Create a durable or deterministically rebuildable projection representing an opportunity.

Each opportunity should have stable identity and enough provenance to audit/rebuild it.

Suggested conceptual fields:

```text
id
repertoire_id
kind
canonical_fen_key
card_id?                 # existing target when applicable
opponent_move_uci?       # missing response when applicable
status
score
evidence_json
created_at
updated_at
resolved_at?
```

Possible statuses should support at least:

- active;
- dismissed;
- resolved/stale as appropriate.

Do not create a generic event-sourcing framework.

Use Tempo's existing derived/background-work conventions.

---

# Actions

Initial opportunity actions should be explicit and user-controlled.

### Weak known decision

Action:

> Promote for training.

This may be automatic if evidence thresholds are conservative and the current admission system supports it safely, but the reason must remain visible.

### Missing common response

Action:

> Investigate / add branch.

Do not automatically write a Stockfish-generated line into the authoritative repertoire in v1.

### Post-gap weakness

Action:

> Review evidence / investigate response.

Where an existing unseen card already matches the needed decision, reuse it.

---

# UI

Add a compact place to inspect actionable repertoire opportunities.

Do not build a large analytics dashboard.

Each item should answer:

1. What position/decision is this?
2. What is missing or weak?
3. Why did Tempo surface it?
4. What evidence supports it?
5. What can I do?

Example:

```text
Weak known decision

Reached: 11 recent games
Correct: 4
Missed: 7
Card status: locked behind earlier prefix

[Promote for training]
```

Example:

```text
Missing response: ...Nh5

Maia 1500: 8.4%
Lichess cohort: 6.9%
Your games: 5 encounters
Coverage: missing

[Investigate branch]
```

Keep provenance visible without overwhelming the normal Train experience.

---

# Background-work requirements

Opportunity discovery is background analysis.

Follow Tempo's foreground-first rules:

- no long SQLite write transactions;
- copy bounded inputs;
- perform chess/probability computation outside write sections;
- publish idempotent derived results;
- yield to foreground training/reviews;
- resume safely after interruption;
- avoid duplicating findings/opportunities after restart.

Integrate with the existing background activity infrastructure so the user can understand that repertoire scouting is running.

---

# Relationship to existing services

Before implementing, trace and reuse:

- `backend/app/services/opening_graph.py`
- `backend/app/services/introduction_priorities.py`
- `backend/app/services/repertoire_coverage.py`
- `backend/app/services/repertoire_comparison.py`
- `backend/app/services/real_game_feedback.py`
- `backend/app/services/game_findings.py`
- `repertoire_decision_events`
- `game_position_occurrences`
- current durable/background task machinery.

Do not build a second coverage engine, second canonical-position model, or second game-matching implementation.

The existing `game_findings.py` post-gap behavior is particularly relevant and should be incorporated rather than duplicated.

---

# Important invariants

1. Gameplay evidence does not fabricate FSRS reviews.
2. Early descendant promotion does not mark ancestors mature.
3. Canonical decision identity survives transpositions.
4. Opponent deviations are not player failures.
5. A missing branch is not silently added to the authoritative repertoire.
6. One source failing (Explorer/Maia/etc.) should not invalidate usable evidence from other sources.
7. Stale/unknown probability evidence must be represented as such.
8. Reprocessing is idempotent.
9. Dismissed opportunities should not immediately regenerate unchanged.
10. Repertoire integrity rules remain authoritative.

---

# Regression coverage

Add named regression coverage and update `tests/REGRESSIONS.md`.

At minimum cover:

### Evidence-backed promotion

- locked descendant with strong route-success + target-miss evidence becomes eligible;
- its ancestors remain unchanged/not mature;
- no synthetic review is created;
- one isolated encounter does not unlock it;
- repeated processing does not duplicate queue entries/evidence;
- explanation/provenance reaches the training projection.

### Transpositions

- equivalent canonical decision reached through different move orders aggregates to the same opportunity/card.

### Known-successful decisions

- frequently reached, consistently successful decision does not become a weakness opportunity merely because it is formally unstudied.

### Missing response

- sufficiently probable uncovered opponent move creates one opportunity;
- covered move does not;
- very low-probability/unobserved move does not create noise;
- personal repeated occurrence can surface a move omitted by Masters;
- missing Masters evidence does not suppress strong Maia/personal evidence.

### Post-gap weakness

- uncovered opponent response followed shortly by a significant player mistake creates/updates one post-gap opportunity;
- existing matching unseen card is linked rather than duplicated;
- repeated derivation is idempotent.

### Source degradation

- unavailable/stale Explorer or Maia evidence is represented honestly;
- other evidence can still support an opportunity where appropriate.

### Dismissal/resolution

- dismissed unchanged opportunity does not immediately reappear;
- materially changed/new evidence may reopen according to an explicit rule.

### Foreground reliability

- large opportunity scan does not block card review/training;
- interrupted scan resumes without duplicate publication.

---

# Suggested staged implementation

This is one product feature but should be implemented incrementally.

### Stage 1 — evidence projection

Build canonical per-decision gameplay summaries and opportunity records.

No major UI beyond diagnostics/tests.

### Stage 2 — weak-known-decision promotion

Allow evidence-backed admission of existing descendants while preserving ancestry and FSRS semantics.

This is the most immediately useful vertical slice.

### Stage 3 — missing-response scouting

Use coverage + Maia + Explorer + personal evidence to produce uncovered-response opportunities.

### Stage 4 — post-gap synthesis

Fold the existing game-finding behavior into the same opportunity model.

### Stage 5 — compact UI/actions

Expose opportunities and explicit actions.

Do not wait until every evidence source is perfect before delivering Stage 2.

---

# Definition of done

The feature is successful when Tempo can support all three scenarios:

### Scenario A: I already know the route but fail later

> I repeatedly play the first six decisions correctly in real games, repeatedly reach decision seven, and repeatedly get decision seven wrong. Tempo can promote decision seven for training even though the formal graph prerequisites are not mature, without pretending those prerequisites have been studied.

### Scenario B: my repertoire ignores a common lower-level response

> Maia, the relevant Lichess cohort, and/or my personal games show an opponent response is practically common, but my repertoire has no branch for it. Tempo surfaces that gap with its evidence and lets me investigate/add coverage.

### Scenario C: I get lost after an uncovered move

> An opponent plays something outside my repertoire and I repeatedly or significantly misplay the following decisions. Tempo identifies the post-gap weakness and surfaces it as an actionable repertoire opportunity.

All recommendations must remain auditable: the user should be able to tell **why Tempo thinks this matters**.

---

# Out of scope

Do not add:

- learned/ML recommendation ranking;
- causal claims about training effectiveness;
- automatic Stockfish-authored repertoire mutation;
- exhaustive legal-move expansion;
- broad FSRS redesign;
- new analytics database;
- generic event-bus architecture;
- major Builder redesign.

The goal is to make existing evidence change the curriculum intelligently while preserving Tempo's current separation between gameplay evidence, study evidence, and repertoire authority.

[PR #58](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/58) and [PR #66](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/66) are merged. They provide preview scheduling, explicit canonical opening scope, certified authoritative route sources, and scope fences for coverage, opportunities and game publications. Shared authored memberships/history, bounded cleanup and actionable manual recheck guidance remain preserved.

[PR #98](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/pull/98) is merged and closes [#7](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/issues/7) and [#8](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/issues/8). It preserves dismissal through transient resolution/staleness until material supporting evidence changes, selects the newest current-scope attempt, independently qualifies Maia/Explorer evidence, and fences publication/checkpoint/cleanup against obsolete sources. Its [successful current-candidate CI](https://github.com/aaweaver-actuary/tempo/actions/runs/37667972027) includes the named OF-1/OF-2 PostgreSQL proofs and complete required verification.
